items.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013
items.q: And I says, “Well, Mary, I wouldn’t be able to do that, because I’m not trained for it.

ctx.x: No I was so respectful. I’d stay out of the way. Because he was the show. I was just a sidekick. They didn’t know who I was and they didn’t really care. They figured I probably was his son. So I was an adjunct to him. He was the one. When we went into some of the white churches the same kind of thing happened. And so I learned all this stuff because of Bill. And he’d give me his notes, he’d show me how to do it and I’d go

visit him all the time. I remember him telling me one time Coltrane was in town and I called him up and I says, “McCoy Tyner just took a twenty-one minute solo.” I used to time everything you know. And he goes, “I can’t do it right now, Chuck, because I’m teaching country and folk and my whole head is in country and folk.” I didn’t understand it at the time. But he did his intro courses, which were the big draws, like my jazz-rock, now American popular music is a big draw. And then he did this special course,…

pretty well. So I had the job pretty much, and then I’ll never forget, I got a call over at Cole’s. And there was one more guy they had to interview. And Tallmadge, he goes, “Chuck, I’ve got to tell you, this crazy guy came in from New York City, his name is Brown, he’s written two books, he has a doctorate, you only have a master’s, and I know you’re working on” — I finished the second master’s in film theory with Jerry O’Grady over at Media Studies. And I did a lot of things on music, film music and blah, blah,…
